title: Level-One Fock Space and Residue Crystals

items.title: The symmetric-group level-one residue and partition-label convention
items.statement:
Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; for prime $e=p$, it agrees with the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the list in reverse order, with the opposite cancellation, and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ of
[[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the operators act on
*all* partitions). When the wedge bar $\psi$ is supplied by the global-basis
construction, transport it by the formula below; this convention does not
construct that bar. The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every $a \ge 1$ the multiplicity of the part $a$ in $\lambda'$ equals $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1}$. Indeed the columns of $[\lambda]$ of height at least $a$ are exactly the first $\lambda_a$ columns, because column $j$ has height $\#\{r : \lambda_r \ge j\} \ge a$ if and only if $j \le \lambda_a$; hence the columns of height exactly $a$ number $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1}$, and these heights are precisely the parts of $\lambda'$ by [F1]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Transposition of nodes: $(r,c) \in [\lambda]$ if and only if $(c,r) \in [\lambda']$, so $(r,c) \mapsto (c,r)$ is a bijection from the nodes of $\lambda$ onto the nodes of $\lambda'$. It preserves addability and removability: deleting $(r,c)$ from $[\lambda]$ leaves the diagram of a partition $\mu$ if and only if deleting $(c,r)$ from $[\lambda']$ leaves the diagram of $\mu'$, and the same argument with diagrams enlarged by one node gives addability. It negates the residue, $\operatorname{res}(c,r) = r - c = -(c-r) = -\operatorname{res}(r,c)$ in $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 Distinct corners of a partition have distinct contents. Let $x = (r,c) \ne y = (s,d)$ be addable or removable nodes with equal content $c - r = d - s$; by [F2] each is of the form $(a,\lambda_a)$ (removable) or $(a,\lambda_a+1)$ (addable, the new bottom row included via $\lambda_{k+1} = 0$). If $r=s$, two distinct corners must be the removable and addable endpoints of that row, whose contents differ by $1$, so they cannot have equal content. Interchange the nodes if needed to take $r<s$. If $x$ and $y$ are both removable with $r < s$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$ while $\lambda_r - r = \lambda_s - s$ forces $\lambda_r - \lambda_s = r - s < 0$, a contradiction. If both are addable with $r < s$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$ while equal contents force $\lambda_r - \lambda_s = r - s < 0$, again a contradiction. If $x$ is removable and $y$ addable with $r < s$, equal contents give $\lambda_r - \lambda_s = r + 1 - s$; for $s \ge r+2$ the right side is at most $-1$, so $\lambda_r < \lambda_s$, contradicting $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$, and for $s = r+1$ it gives $\lambda_r = \lambda_s$, which contradicts the addability of $(s,\lambda_s+1)$, that is $\lambda_{s-1} = \lambda_r > \lambda_s$ (here $s \ge 2$ because $r \ge 1$). If $x$ is addable with smaller row $r$ than the removable $y = (s,\lambda_s)$, then $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$ while $\lambda_r + 1 - r = \lambda_s - s$ forces $\lambda_s - \lambda_r = s + 1 - r \ge 2$, contradicting $\lambda_r \ge \lambda_s$. All possible pairs are covered, so equal contents force $x = y$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Consequently $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted, i.e. $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for all $a$, if and only if the part $a$ occurs in $\lambda'$ fewer than $e$ times, i.e. $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: step 1.1 identifies the two lists of integers compared with $e$. For $\lambda = \varnothing$, where $\lambda_a = 0$ for all $a$, both conditions are the empty family of inequalities and both hold; for $a > k$ one has $\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} = 0 < e$, so the restrictedness condition is finite, and $m_i(\varnothing) = 0$ for all $i$. [given, step 1.1, F3, F4]

2.2 Step 1.2 also gives the weight bookkeeping: the transposition bijects the residue-$i$ nodes of $\lambda$ onto the residue-$(-i)$ nodes of $\lambda'$, so $m_i(\lambda) = m_{-i}(\lambda')$ for every $i$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda'\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_j(\lambda')\alpha_j = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_{-j}(\lambda)\alpha_j = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda))$: applying the transposition of labels to the weight is the reflection $i \mapsto -i$ on the coefficients. In particular the relabelled basis vector $M_\lambda$ is a weight vector of weight $\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda)$ for the transported toral action, since $K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} M_\lambda = J^{-1}K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J M_\lambda = q^{\langle \tau h, \operatorname{wt}(|\lambda'\rangle)\rangle} M_\lambda = q^{\langle h, \tau\, \operatorname{wt}(|\lambda'\rangle)\rangle} M_\lambda = q^{\langle h, \operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda)\rangle} M_\lambda$, using that $\tau$ preserves the pairing and exchanges $h_j$ with $h_{-j}$ ([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). [given, step 1.2, F1, F4, algebra]

2.3 The transported operators act by node moves with reflected colors. For any partition $\mu$, the QG operator $E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}$ sends $|\mu\rangle$ to a linear combination of $|\mu \setminus \gamma\rangle$ over the removable nodes $\gamma$ of $\mu$ of residue $-i$, and $F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}$ sends $|\mu\rangle$ to a combination of $|\mu \cup \beta\rangle$ over the addable nodes $\beta$ of $\mu$ of residue $-i$ ([[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]]); conjugating by $J$ and using step 1.2, $E_i^{\mathrm{sym}}$ sends $M_\lambda$ ($J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle$) to the $J^{-1}$-images of the results of removing residue-$(-i)$ removable nodes of $\lambda'$, that is, to combinations of $M_{\lambda \setminus \gamma}$ over the removable nodes $\gamma$ of $\lambda$ of residue $i$, and likewise $F_i^{\mathrm{sym}}$ adds residue-$i$ nodes of $\lambda$. Thus at the level of nodes the symmetric-group model uses the same residue labels as the modular signature of the Definition, not their negatives. [given, step 1.2, F1, F2, F4]

2.4 At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ the colors form the set $I = \mathbb{Z}$ and, by [F2] and step 1.3, each residue class contains at most one node of $\lambda$: an $i$-node is a corner of content exactly $i$, and there is at most one such corner. Hence the residue word of every color has length at most one, no cancellation can occur, and for every nonempty $\lambda$ the removable corner $(k,\lambda_k)$ of its last row is the good node of its own residue, so repeated good deletions carry $\lambda$ to $\varnothing$; consult the $e = 0$ case of the survey's level-one example, under which every level-one partition is a crystal label. No finite affine datum, charge or weight formula is asserted here. [given, step 1.3, F2]

3.1 The conjugation $C(\lambda) = \lambda'$ is a bijection from the $e$-restricted partition class onto the $e$-regular class by step 2.1, and it is not an involution of the $e$-restricted class: at $e = 3$ it sends the restricted shape $(1,1,1)$ to the non-restricted shape $(3)$, and at $e = 2$ it sends the restricted shape $(1,1,1,1)$ to the non-restricted shape $(4)$; the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of the survey instead preserves the restricted label set and is computed by negating the residues of a good-node path inside it. In the group regime the published dictionary for conjugate-sign duality of simple labels is exactly the stated identification $D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]). [given, step 2.1, step 1.2] ∎

items.title: Residue-node reading orders and the conjugation dictionary
items.statement: For distinct addable/removable corners of one residue i (finite e≥2), smaller row implies strictly larger column and strictly larger content. Hence top-to-bottom=DECREASING content=decreasing column; bottom-to-top=increasing content. A same-residue row or column cannot repeat. Conjugation sends a top-to-bottom i-corner list of lambda to the bottom-to-top (increasing content) −i-corner list of lambda-prime, preserving signs. Thus its modular −+ cancellations, FIRST− good deletion and LAST+ cogood addition agree exactly with the QG INCREASING-content −+ rule on lambda-prime. Equivalently reverse the latter list and use decreasing-content +− cancellation, LAST− deletion and FIRST+ addition. Both versions select the same actual nodes. They apply to all partitions as signatures; the basic graph restriction is imposed separately.
items.strategy: Let rows r<s. Boundary inequalities give c_r≥c_s: check removable/removable, addable/addable, addable/removable directly from weak row lengths; for removable/addable, the upper removable drop and lower addability give the same weak inequality. Equality is possible for mixed types, so the native general 'impossible' assertion was false. If a removable upper corner and an addable lower corner share a column, their rows must be adjacent at that column's boundary, hence their contents differ1; the reverse mixed orientation cannot share a column. Equal-row mixed corners also differ1 in content. Same-residue e≥2 excludes these exceptions. Strict columns and r<s imply strictly DECREASING content. Conjugating exchanges rows/columns and negates content, yielding the stated order reversal. Stack reduction of −+ is uniquely determined: scan with a minus stack, cancel each plus with the last unmatched minus; reversing the word yields +− with first/last extrema reversed. Therefore the surviving-node bijection and selected-node identities are exact, not only an abstract isomorphism. This is the full elementary proof supplementing Fayers §4, whose text records the conventions but omits proofs.

items.title: The QG Fock-crystal arrows are the modular good-node operators
items.statement:
Consider the modular reading on the one hand (the top-to-bottom residue
signature with good $=$ first surviving $-$ and cogood $=$ last surviving $+$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], whose
operators delete the good node and add the cogood node on $e$-restricted
labels) and the level-one Fock crystal $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$,
$\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_i$ on the other. Conjugation
$C(\lambda) = \lambda'$ sends the modular operators on $e$-restricted
partitions onto the normalized operators of the **empty connected component** of
the QG full partition Fock crystal, with the colors negated:
$$C\,\tilde e_i\lambda = \tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda, \qquad C\,\tilde f_i\lambda = \tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda \qquad (\lambda\ e\text{-restricted}),$$
including the zero values: the left side is zero exactly when the right side is.
The survivor counts are the same on both sides,
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\lambda')$ and
$\varphi_i(\lambda) = \varphi_{-i}(\lambda')$, and the weight transforms by the
diagram reflection, $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda') = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(\lambda))$.
With the transported full module $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], the
modular signatures likewise give its normalized operators on **all** partitions
(the transported operators $J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$,
$J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$), and the restricted subset of that full
crystal is its basic component. In both conventions good means removable
(deletion, $\tilde e$) and cogood means addable (addition, $\tilde f$): there is
no opposite naming-polarity dictionary exchanging deletion with addition.
Ordinary Chevalley coefficients, especially negative powers such as $q^{-1}$,
do not define these arrows.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For every partition $\mu$ and every color $i$, the selection operations of the two readings correspond under transposition. By [F2] the top-to-bottom $i$-node word of $\mu$ equals the increasing-content $(-i)$-node word of $\mu'$ position by position, with the same signs, so the reduced survivor words coincide; consequently $\varepsilon_i(\mu) = \varepsilon_{-i}(\mu')$ and $\varphi_i(\mu) = \varphi_{-i}(\mu')$, and if $\varepsilon_i(\mu) > 0$ then the good $i$-node of $\mu$ is the transposed node of the good $(-i)$-node of $\mu'$, while if $\varphi_i(\mu) > 0$ then the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$ is the transposed node of the cogood $(-i)$-node of $\mu'$. In particular $\varepsilon_i(\mu) = 0$ if and only if $\varepsilon_{-i}(\mu') = 0$. [given, F2]

1.2 There is no naming-polarity swap between the two conventions: in the modular reading the good node is by definition removable and the cogood node addable ([F1]), in the $p$-restricted operator definition the good node is removable and the cogood node addable ([F3]), and in the Fock-space reading the good node is the surviving $-$, hence removable, while the cogood node is the surviving $+$, hence addable ([F4]); the normalized Fock operators remove the good node and add the cogood node ([F5]). Hence both dictionaries compare a deletion with a deletion and an addition with an addition, and the only change is the color reflection $i \mapsto -i$. [given, F3, F4, F5]

2.1 The transported crystal operators on all partition residues are given by the modular signature rule. The field operators $J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$ and $J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$ preserve $(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$ by [F5]; let $b_\mu:=M_\mu+q(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$. The induced map of residue spaces sends $b_\mu$ to $|\mu'\rangle+qF_0$. By [F4]-[F5] its raising image is the residue of the partition obtained by deleting the good $(-i)$-node of $\mu'$, or zero when no such node exists. Step 1.1 identifies that node with the transpose of the modular good $i$-node $A$ of $\mu$, so $\tilde e_i^{\mathrm{sym}}b_\mu=b_{\mu\setminus A}$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and zero otherwise. The same argument gives $\tilde f_i^{\mathrm{sym}}b_\mu=b_{\mu\cup B}$ for the modular cogood node $B$, and zero when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. These are equalities of crystal residues: on raw standard vectors they assert congruences modulo $q(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$, including at zero arrows, rather than exact field-vector equalities. [given, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 Weights transform by the reflection. By [F1] the transported weight satisfies $\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\mu)\alpha_i$ and $m_i(\mu) = m_{-i}(\mu')$; hence $\operatorname{wt}(|\mu'\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_j(\mu')\alpha_j = \Lambda_0 - \sum_j m_{-j}(\mu)\alpha_j = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu))$, and the weight of a crystal arrow is preserved by the node moves of step 2.1 because those moves change one residue count by one on each side consistently. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Restricted case. Let $\lambda$ be $e$-restricted, so that $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular by [F1] and hence a vertex of the empty component of the full Fock crystal by [F5], on which the operators $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}$, $\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}$ of [F5] act. By step 2.1 applied at $\mu = \lambda$, the modular operator $\tilde e_i$ on $\lambda$ (delete the good $i$-node, zero if $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) = 0$) is intertwined with $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}$ on $\lambda'$: $C\,\tilde e_i\lambda = \tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda$, and likewise $C\,\tilde f_i\lambda = \tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}C\lambda$, both sides being zero together by the count agreement of step 1.1. Since transposition is a bijection from the $e$-restricted onto the $e$-regular labels and [F5] identifies the latter precisely as the vertex set of the empty component, the conjugation of the modular restricted graph is exactly that empty component, with colors negated; for $e = p$ prime the modular side is the operator system of [F3], and in general it is the reading fixed in [F1]. [given, F1, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Finally, the arrows are not read off from ordinary Chevalley coefficients. The selection is the signature reduction of [F4], and [F4]-[F5] record that a pole or a unique Chevalley term does not determine the crystal arrow; the transported operator $\tilde e^{\mathrm{sym}}_i$ of step 2.1 is the normalization inherited from $\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}$, not the transported Chevalley operator $E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} = J^{-1}E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}J$, whose coefficients (such as $q^{-1}$ from the formulas of Leclerc (38)-(39)) differ from the arrow data. [given, F4, F5, step 2.1] ∎

items.title: The restricted-partition component is the basic crystal in the symmetric-group convention
items.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice exactly through [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]], which uses it to split an integrable module with a crystal basis into highest-weight components; the identification of the empty component with the $e$-restricted partitions themselves is choice-free (Kleshchev Theorem 8.2(ii) with Example 3.2(i) and Fayers' restricted model are direct constructions of the crystal on that vertex set). The choice-free alternative is recorded in the strategy.
items.statement:
Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$. In the symmetric-group convention of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]:

1. The empty component of the transported full Fock crystal $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
   is **exactly the set of $e$-restricted partitions**, its operators are the
   modular good-node deletions and cogood-node additions, its weight function is
   $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, the
   counts $\varepsilon_i$, $\varphi_i$ are the numbers of normal and of
   conormal $i$-nodes, and the component is $B(\Lambda_0)$: every $e$-restricted
   shape is reached from the empty partition by successive cogood additions.
2. The full $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has all partitions as vertices and is reducible;
   its transported field decomposition is
   $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \cong \bigoplus_{k \ge 0} V(\Lambda_0 - k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)}$
   with $p(k)$ the number of partitions of $k$, so its other vertices are
   exactly the non-restricted shapes.
3. In the symmetric-group regime (algebraically closed field $k$ of
   characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so $e = p$ is prime) the
   $e$-restricted labels $\lambda$ are the simple $kS_d$-modules in the
   dual-Specht convention, and for every $i$ with $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$
   $$\operatorname{soc}\bigl(E_{-i}D^{\lambda'}\bigr) = D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'},$$
   where $D^{\lambda'}$ is the James-labelled simple, $E_{-i}$ the
   residue-summand functor after the sign twist, and $D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'}$
   the James label of the deleted shape. That is, the standard $E_{-i}$ is the
   residue functor twisted by the sign representation.
4. At quantum characteristic $e = 0$ (colors $\mathbb{Z}$) every level-one
   partition is a label of the empty $\mathfrak{sl}_\infty$ crystal, there are
   no same-content corner cancellations, and no finite affine datum, weight
   formula or Hecke module statement is made.

General finite-$e$ Hecke crystal labels remain valid, but they are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". The axiom of choice is used
exactly as declared in the contract, through the highest-weight decomposition of
the full Fock module; the vertex-set identification and signature reachability in part 1 are
choice-free. The proof below also uses the declared choice-bearing supplier
to identify the component with the canonical highest-weight crystal.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The conjugation dictionary identifies the vertex sets of the two components. By [F1] transposition is a bijection from the $e$-restricted onto the $e$-regular partitions, fixing the empty partition, and by [F3] the vertex set of the empty component of the full Fock crystal is exactly the set of $e$-regular partitions. Hence the $J^{-1}$-image of the empty component is exactly the $e$-restricted set, with the empty partition corresponding to the vacuum, and by [F2] the transported modular operators on these labels are the transported normalized Fock operators $\tilde e^{\mathrm{sym}}_i = J^{-1}\tilde e^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$, $\tilde f^{\mathrm{sym}}_i = J^{-1}\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}_{-i}J$. [given, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 The transported component is connected and generated from the vacuum. The empty component of [F3] is the canonical $B(\Lambda_0)$, hence connected and generated from its highest vertex by the $\tilde f^{\mathrm{QG}}$; transporting along the bijection of step 1.1, the $e$-restricted labels form one connected component of the transported crystal, generated from the empty partition by the operators $\tilde f^{\mathrm{sym}}_i$, that is, by modular cogood additions. In particular every $e$-restricted shape is reached from the empty partition by successive cogood additions, and dually by successive good deletions; for $e = p$ prime this is also the choice-free statement of [F4], whose good and cogood nodes are the modular ones by [F2]. [given, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1]

2.2 The weight function is the transported one. By [F1] the weight of $M_\lambda$ is $\Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$ with $m_i(\lambda)$ the number of residue-$i$ nodes, and by [F2] it transforms under conjugation as $\operatorname{wt}(\lambda') = \tau(\operatorname{wt}(\lambda))$; the vacuum $\varnothing$ has weight $\Lambda_0$ since $m_i(\varnothing) = 0$. The modular $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ are by construction the numbers of surviving $-$ and $+$, that is, of normal removable and conormal addable $i$-nodes in the sense of the modular signature. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 This proves part 1 of the Statement: the empty component of $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is exactly the $e$-restricted partitions (step 1.1), its operators are the modular good deletions and cogood additions (step 1.1), its weight is $\Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$ (step 2.2), $\varepsilon$, $\varphi$ count normal and conormal nodes (step 2.2), and it is $B(\Lambda_0)$ with every restricted shape reached from the empty partition by cogood additions (step 2.1). [given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 For part 2, the full $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ has all partitions as vertices and its module is the transport of the modules of [F3], so its field decomposition is $F_{\mathrm{sym}} \cong \bigoplus_{k\ge0} V(\Lambda_0 - k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)}$ with $p(k)$ ordinary partition numbers; this direct sum is infinite, so $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$ is reducible whenever at least two summands are nonzero (for instance the summands $V(\Lambda_0)$ and $V(\Lambda_0-\delta)$). Since the empty component is exactly the $e$-restricted shapes by step 3.1, every other vertex of the full crystal is a non-restricted shape, and conversely each non-restricted shape lies outside the empty component. The axiom of choice is inherited through [F3], both here for the field decomposition and in steps 1.1-2.1 for the canonical highest-weight-crystal identification. The transport itself introduces no choice. The vertex-set identification and reachability can also be read directly from the choice-free partition-graph supplier of [F2], and [F4] gives the prime-case reachability without choice. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1]

4.2 Part 3, the James labels and the socle formula. Let $k$ be of characteristic $p > 0$ and $e = p$; $e$-restricted $\lambda$ are exactly the labels $D(\lambda)$ of the simple $kS_d$-modules in the dual-Specht convention, and for $p$-regular $\lambda'$ the published dictionary gives $D^{\lambda'} \cong D(\lambda) \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ by [F6]. Suppose $\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$ and let $A$ be the good $i$-node, so that $\tilde e_i\lambda = \lambda \setminus A$ and, by [F5], $\operatorname{soc} E_iD(\lambda) \cong D(\lambda\setminus A)$. Tensoring with $\operatorname{sgn}$ negates the Jucys-Murphy action: for $v \otimes w$ in $M \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, $L_r(v\otimes w) = \sum_{s<r}((s\,r)v) \otimes ((s\,r)w) = -L_r v \otimes w$ because each $(s\,r)$ acts by $-1$ on $\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F6]; hence the content vector of the sign twist is the negative, and by [F5] the residue summands satisfy $E_{-i}\bigl(M \otimes \operatorname{sgn}\bigr) \cong (E_iM) \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$. The twist is an exact invertible endofunctor (its square is the identity on isomorphism classes), so it preserves socles and simples; applying it to $\operatorname{soc} E_iD(\lambda) \cong D(\lambda\setminus A)$ gives $\operatorname{soc}\bigl(E_{-i}(D(\lambda)\otimes\operatorname{sgn})\bigr) \cong D(\lambda\setminus A) \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, and the two published re-identifications $D(\lambda)\otimes\operatorname{sgn} \cong D^{\lambda'}$ and $D(\lambda\setminus A)\otimes\operatorname{sgn} \cong D^{(\lambda\setminus A)'}$ of [F6] yield $\operatorname{soc} E_{-i}D^{\lambda'} \cong D^{(\tilde e_i\lambda)'}$; this is the stated formula, and it exhibits $E_{-i}$ as the sign twist of the residue functor $E_i$. [given, F5, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 Part 4, the boundary and the naming caveats. At $e = 0$ the colors are $\mathbb{Z}$ and, by [F7] together with the distinct-content computation recorded in the convention item [[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]], each residue class contains at most one corner of a partition, so no signature contains a cancellable pair; every partition reaches the empty partition by good deletions, and the source's restricted set for level $1$ is all partitions. No finite affine datum, charge, weight formula or symmetric-group module statement is made in this boundary; and for a general finite $e \ge 2$ the crystal labels of parts 1 and 2 are Hecke labels, valid for any quantum characteristic $e$, not only for prime $e$ as in part 3. [given, F7, step 3.1, step 4.2] ∎

items.title: Level-one global-basis transition polynomials in the symmetric-group convention
items.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice through [[thm-the-basic-representation-global-basis-is-unitriangular-in-the-partition-basis]] (and hence through [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]) for the decomposition of the Fock space into highest-weight components; the definition of the polynomials themselves and the pairing are choice-free. Consumers must carry the same assumption while it is used.
items.statement:
Work in the linear symmetric-group model of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]: the
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $J M_\mu = |\mu'\rangle$, the transported
action, bar and $A_0$ standard chart $(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$, and the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\mu)\alpha_i$, with
$A = \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$.

**The basic module and its lower basis.** Let
$M_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1}V(\Lambda_0) = J^{-1}M_{\mathrm{QG}}$ be the
transported highest-weight module of the vacuum; by
[[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]
its crystal is the $e$-restricted component and its labels are the $e$-restricted
partitions. For an $e$-restricted $\lambda$ define
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) := J^{-1}G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda'),$$
where $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\mu)$ is the lower global (canonical) basis element of
the Fock space at the standard vector $|\mu\rangle$
([[thm-the-basic-representation-global-basis-is-unitriangular-in-the-partition-basis]]).
Then $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) \equiv M_\lambda \bmod q\,(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$
and the family $\{G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)\}$ is the transported lower global
basis of $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$, indexed by the restricted labels. Define the
**level-one transition polynomials in the symmetric-group convention** by the
finite weightwise expansion
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) = \sum_\mu d_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q)\, M_\mu ,$$
the sum being over the partitions $\mu$ of the weight of $\lambda$.

**Ambient polarization and ambient upper coordinates.** Define the ambient
polarization by $B(M_\mu,M_\nu) = \delta_{\mu\nu}$ on the standard basis, a
symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each finite weight space. Fix a weight
$w$ and let $V_w$ be the (finite-dimensional) weight space of
$F_{\mathrm{sym}}$; let $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ be the matrix with columns the
coordinate vectors of $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)$ for the finitely many
$e$-restricted $\lambda$ of weight $w$, and rows the **standard** shapes
$M_\mu$, $\mu$ of weight $w$; let
$$H := D_{\mathrm{rect}}^{\mathsf{t}}\, D_{\mathrm{rect}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda) := \sum_\mu \bigl(D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1}\bigr)_{(\mu,\lambda)}\, M_\mu^* ,$$
where $M_\mu^*$ denotes the ambient orthonormal dual frame of the standard
basis. The $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda)$ are the **ambient upper coordinates**
of the basic module: they are the unique elements of the basic subspace
$(M_{\mathrm{sym}})_w\subseteq V_w$ characterized weightwise by $B(G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda), G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda')) = \delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$,
and are viewed in the ambient standard frame; adding a vector of the
$B$-orthogonal complement in $V_w$ gives other ambient representatives with
the same pairings. The coefficients
$e_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q) := (D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1})_{(\mu,\lambda)}$ lie in
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$ but need not be Laurent integral or polynomial. They are
coordinates in the ambient space and not a "standard basis of the basic
module"; the exact integral upper basis is the transported upper global basis of
[[thm-upper-and-lower-global-bases-are-dual-and-crystal-compatible]], whose
restricted graded $A$-dual lattice is free weightwise and perfectly paired with
the basic lower $A$-span, while no lower-$A$ selfduality, no $A$-unit $H$ and no
full algebraic duality in infinite rank is implied. The restriction of $B$ to the basic module equals the normalized transported
contravariant form (proved in step 4.2), so these are the same upper vectors
viewed in the ambient standard frame and in their own integral dual lattice.
Upper bar is the adjoint bar
$\psi^\vee$ with its own dual infinity chart and weighted upper operators, not
the ordinary lower bar.

**The full ambient case.** On the whole Fock space the analogous matrix
$D_{\mathrm{full}}$, with columns the $G(\mu)$ over all partitions and rows the
standard shapes, is unitriangular (diagonal $1$, in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$ below the
diagonal), and the dual matrix with respect to $B$ is
$$D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}},$$
which is Laurent integral because the inverse of a unitriangular matrix with
entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$.

**A worked instance.** At $e = 2$ the restricted shape $\lambda = (1,1)$ has
$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1) = M_{1,1} + q\,M_{2}$, so $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ has the
single column $(q,1)^{\mathsf{t}}$, $H = 1 + q^2$, and
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1) = \frac{M_{1,1}^* + q\,M_2^*}{1+q^2} = \frac{M_{1,1} + q\,M_2}{1+q^2},$$
an explicit ambient coordinate that is rational but not Laurent integral:
$1 + q^2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$. No specialization of the $d$
to decomposition numbers of Hecke algebras is asserted here without the
separate correct Hecke parameter hypotheses.
items.strategy: Transport the lower Fock basis by the linear transpose-label map J, preserving q; obtain the exact coefficient identity, symmetric dominance direction, same-core and full reflected-weight support. Work weightwise with the rectangular lower-column matrix D and ambient orthonormal form. D(0) has distinct coordinate columns, so H=D^tD satisfies H(0)=I and is field invertible; DH^-1 gives the unique upper vectors inside the basic subspace, with whole-ambient representatives differing by its orthogonal complement. Compute the e=2 rational coordinates and the full ambient transpose-inverse matrix separately. The finite node-count identity Nright+Nleft=N(lambda)-1 proves sigma-adjointness of the orthonormal form; normalized highest-weight form uniqueness identifies its basic restriction with the transported QG form. Thus these upper vectors form the restricted integral dual basis with perfect pairing, while rational standard coordinates imply neither lower-A selfduality nor an A-unit Gram matrix. Transport the exact adjoint upper bar, dual charts and weighted operators; preserve all linear/semilinear and Hecke-parameter boundaries.

items.title: General Hecke cellular simple labels match the basic crystal
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice only for the canonical basic-component identification through [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]. The finite recursive cellular comparison adds no use of Choice.

Let $F$ be any field, $q\in F^\times$ of finite quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, and use the Murphy restricted labels $D(\lambda)$ and residue functors $E_i,F_i$ of [[lem-general-hecke-residue-branching-endpoints-from-normalized-schur-cells]], with residue $c-r\bmod e$. Recursively set $\dot D(\varnothing)=F$ and $\dot D(\lambda)=\operatorname{hd}F_i\dot D(\widetilde e_i\lambda)$ for any defined good deletion. This is defined at every restricted partition, independent of the selected deletion, and $\dot D(\lambda)\cong D(\lambda)$. This finite recursive comparison holds without Choice; only the canonical basic-component identification below assumes Choice. The finite recursive comparison adds no Choice use and does not use Fock-space classification to identify a module head. These restricted labels, with the displayed good/cogood operators, are the transported basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with weight $\Lambda_0-\sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The basic-component assertion carries the declared Choice in the integrable crystal decomposition of [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]]. The assertion is for level-one type-A Hecke algebras; it supplies no arbitrary-level cyclotomic label theorem.
items.strategy:
1.1 For a partition $\lambda$, list addable pluses and removable minuses of residue $i$ from top to bottom and cancel $-+$ pairs by a last-in-first-out minus stack. Deleting the first surviving minus and adding the last surviving plus are inverse selected moves. Indeed changing the selected corner changes its sign; every other altered boundary corner has residue $i+1$ or $i-1$, different from $i$ even at $e=2$. Immediately before a first surviving minus the minus stack is empty, and every suffix prefix has at least as many remaining minus pushes as plus pops. After flipping that minus to plus, these conditions say precisely that this plus survives and no later plus does. Reversing the flip proves the converse. This retains the positions of the selected signs, not just their counts. [given, algebra]

2.1 Good deletion preserves restrictedness. For a removable row $r$, only its gap and the gap immediately above can change: the former decreases by one and the latter increases by one. The only possible violation is $r>1$ and $\lambda_{r-1}-\lambda_r=e-1$. Then the removable corners in rows $r-1,r$ have equal residues, and their minus signs are adjacent in that residue word: the addable corners between them have residues differing by one. If the lower minus survives, the upper one also survives, since stack pops remove the lower minus first. The lower one therefore cannot be the first surviving minus. Cogood addition preserves restrictedness by the dual adjacent-plus argument: if its row gap were $e-1$, the later same-residue addable corner would survive whenever the earlier one did, contradicting selection of the last surviving plus. Hence step 1.1 gives inverse partial operations on the restricted vertex set. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Every nonempty restricted partition has a good deletion. Let $h$ be its height. Its bottom removable node has residue $\lambda_h-h$, while the only boundary node below it is the addable $(h+1,1)$ of residue $-h$. The difference $\lambda_h$ lies strictly between zero and $e$, so these residues differ. There is consequently no later same-residue plus to cancel that bottom minus. At least one minus survives in that residue, and its first surviving minus is a good node. By step 2.1 its deletion stays restricted. Repeating decreases the number of boxes and ends at the empty diagram; reversing gives cogood additions by step 1.1. All selections may be made by the least residue and then the prescribed extremal sign, using finite sets. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Induct on rank to establish both definition and comparison simultaneously. At rank zero the two modules are $F$. Suppose comparison has been established for every smaller rank and let $\lambda$ be nonempty and restricted. Step 3.1 gives a defined predecessor, so the recursion has at least one option. For any allowed residue $i$, put $\mu=\widetilde e_i\lambda$. The induction hypothesis identifies the actual lower-rank module $\dot D(\mu)$ with $D(\mu)$; by steps 1.1 and 2.1 its cogood addition is $\widetilde f_i\mu=\lambda$. Thus [F1] identifies the recursively chosen head with the same simple module $D(\lambda)$ for every allowed $i$. This proves choice independence, existence and the displayed isomorphism at this rank and therefore at every rank. No comparison is used to prove the supplier's cellular endpoint, and no combinatorial connectedness alone identifies a module head. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 By [F2] the restricted graph on these same shapes, with color $i$ and its prescribed good/cogood operations, is the transported canonical $B(\Lambda_0)$ and has the displayed weight. Step 4.1 identifies its recursively attached module at every vertex with the actual Murphy cellular simple. Thus the cellular and basic-crystal labels agree, while the endpoint producer itself used no crystal label comparison. The graph and finite recursive arguments add no Choice; the only inherited use is [F2]'s integrable crystal decomposition, as stated. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: The Fock E- and F-actions on the shape (2,1) at e = 3
items.statement:
At $e = 3$, charge $0$, the quantum-group standard vector $|2,1\rangle$ has
$$F_0|2,1\rangle = |2,2\rangle, \qquad F_1|2,1\rangle = q^{-1}|2,1,1\rangle, \qquad F_2|2,1\rangle = |3,1\rangle,$$
$$E_0|2,1\rangle = 0, \qquad E_1|2,1\rangle = q^{-1}|1,1\rangle, \qquad E_2|2,1\rangle = |2\rangle .$$
The transported symmetric-group standard vector $M_{2,1} = J^{-1}|2,1\rangle$
(the shape is self-conjugate) satisfies
$$F_0^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = M_{2,2}, \qquad F_1^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = M_{2,1,1}, \qquad F_2^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = q^{-1}M_{3,1},$$
$$E_0^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = 0, \qquad E_1^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = M_{1,1}, \qquad E_2^{\mathrm{sym}}M_{2,1} = q^{-1}M_{2},$$
because $J$ transposes the outputs **and** reflects the colors: the operators
used are $F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} = J^{-1}F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}J$ and
$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} = J^{-1}E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}}J$ of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]].

The normalized quantum-group crystal at $2,1$ has arrows
$$\tilde f_0 \to 2,2, \quad \tilde f_1 \to 2,1,1, \quad \tilde e_1 \to 1,1, \qquad \tilde f_2 = \tilde e_2 = 0,$$
while the restricted symmetric model at $2,1$ has instead
$$\tilde f_0 \to 2,2, \quad \tilde f_2 \to 3,1, \quad \tilde e_2 \to 2, \qquad \tilde f_1 = \tilde e_1 = 0 .$$
The raw vector $2,1$ is the representative of its crystal residue in each
model; an ordinary coefficient such as the $q^{-1}$ in $F_1$ or $F_2^{\mathrm{sym}}$
does not refute that, and the Chevalley action of $E_i$, $F_i$ is not their
normalized Kashiwara action.
items.strategy: QG corners have addable(1,3)res2,(2,2)res0,(3,1)res1 and removable(1,2)res1,(2,1)res2. For F1 the bottom addition sees one removable1 on its right, exponent−1. E1 computes N_l on the smaller11, giving1 and coefficientq^-1; E2 on smaller2 gives0. Other coefficients are1. In decreasing-content QG order the color1 word−+ survives, selecting e at the top− and f at the bottom+; color2 word+− cancels, so both normalized arrows vanish although its ordinary F2/E2 are nonzero. The fixed-residue finite tensor cube proves this distinction at the actual raw A0 chart, not through invented global corrections. Apply J^-1 and negate color to the module table: QG211 transposes31 and QG31 transposes211; for i_sym1 use i_QG2, giving M211, and for i_sym2 use i_QG1, givingq^-1M31. The signature lemma gives the stated restricted crystal table. Leclerc Exercise15 is a calibration of the same SMALLER-diagram exponent convention, not this printed example.

items.title: The charge-zero level-one crystal through rank four at e = 3
items.statement: At $e=3$, charge $\Lambda_0$, in the symmetric-group convention, the empty component through rank four has exactly the following vertices, one row per rank: rank $0$: $\varnothing$; rank $1$: $(1)$; rank $2$: $(2)$ and $(1,1)$; rank $3$: $(2,1)$ and $(1,1,1)$; rank $4$: $(3,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(2,1,1)$ and $(1,1,1,1)$. These are exactly the $3$-restricted partitions of each size ($1,1,2,2,4$ of them). The cogood-addition arrows staying within ranks0–4 are: $\varnothing\xrightarrow{\tilde f_0}(1)$; $(1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_1}(2)$, $(1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(1,1)$; $(2)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(2,1)$; $(1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_1}(1,1,1)$; $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_0}(2,2)$, $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(3,1)$; $(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_0}(1,1,1,1)$, $(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_1}(2,1,1)$; All other additions from ranks0–3 vanish; additions from rank4 leaving the displayed window are omitted, not declared zero. The good-deletion arrows into the listed ranks are: $(1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_0}\varnothing$; $(2)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_1}(1)$, $(1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_2}(1)$; $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_2}(2)$, $(1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_1}(1,1)$; $(2,2)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_0}(2,1)$, $(3,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_2}(2,1)$, $(2,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_1}(1,1,1)$, $(1,1,1,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde e_0}(1,1,1)$. In particular $(2,1)$ has no arrow of residue $1$ in either direction, and $(2,1)\xrightarrow{\tilde f_2}(3,1)$ is the arrow whose conjugate is the QG-6 Fock arrow $\tilde f_1$ from $(2,1)$ to $(2,1,1)$.
items.strategy: Finite verification by the reduced $i$-signature, hand-checkable at every vertex. Compute for each listed partition and each $i\in\{0,1,2\}$ the residues $c-r$, list the addable and removable $i$-nodes from top to bottom, cancel $-$ above $+$ pairs and read the topmost surviving $-$ and the bottommost surviving $+$. For example at $(1,1)$ and $i=1$ the two addable nodes $(1,2)$ and $(3,1)$ both survive, giving $\tilde f_1(1,1)=(1,1,1)$; at $(2,1)$ and $i=1$ the removable node $(1,2)$ lies above the addable node $(3,1)$ and the pair cancels, so $\varepsilon_1=\varphi_1=0$ and both arrows vanish; at $(2,1)$ and $i=2$ the addable node $(1,3)$ lies above the removable node $(2,1)$, the word $+-$ does not cancel, and $\tilde f_2(2,1)=(3,1)$, $\tilde e_2(2,1)=(2)$. Residue labels are $c-r$ as fixed in the convention item. The list of $3$-restricted partitions is the direct check of $\lambda_a-\lambda_{a+1}<3$; the count $1,1,2,2,4$ matches the multiplicity of $V(\Lambda_0)$ (Leclerc, *Fock space representations of U_q(sl_n^)*, sec. 3.14, printed pp. 25-26, where the $n$-regular labels give the basic representation; the restricted reading is the transpose/sign dictionary of the convention item). No module theory is used beyond the vertex list of [[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]. The rank4 outgoing boundary is deliberately omitted; completeness/zero claims concern only ranks0–3. This derived finite signature calculation is not a claimed printed native source example.

items.title: The full Fock space is not automatically the irreducible basic module
items.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice through [[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]] and [[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]] for the identification of the basic labels and the top-isotypic lattice splitting; the exhibited non-containment facts themselves are finite checks.
items.statement: At e3 the entire F_sym is strictly larger than its cyclic basic module. The shape4 is not3-restricted since4−0≥3; its conjugate is1111 (NOT111), which is not3-regular since part1 has multiplicity4≥3. Both raw M4 in F_sym and |1111> in F_QG are nonzero and are OUTSIDE their respective field basic modules, and their ambient lower global lifts are outside too. The full signature rule remains meaningful on these shapes in the full Fock crystal; for example restricted-model e0(4)=3 is an edge of another component, not a route into the empty component. Modular/basic signature statements restricted to restricted labels do not apply to4 as a basic label.
items.strategy: Restricted/regular and transposed size checks are immediate. To prove actual vector exclusion rather than graph-only exclusion, apply the actual top-isotypic crystal-lattice splitting theorem to F_QG at its maximal one-dimensional top Lambda0: F0_QG∩V(Lambda0) is the canonical lower lattice and its residue basis exactly the regular empty component. If raw1111 were in this module, its nonzero nonregular residue would lie in that component's span, contradicting residue-basis splitting. Its ambient lower lift has the same residue and is also excluded. Transport by the genuine field and chart isomorphism J gives M4 and its lift. At4, the sole removable0 node is(1,4), so the full restricted signature yields e0→3; neither shape is in the restricted empty component (3−0≥3), hence this edge is compatible with the full decomposable crystal. This corrects the native assertion that the signature had no ambient crystal meaning, while preserving the modular restricted-vertex hypothesis and the strongest field-vector boundary. The splitting applies to the integrable chosen type-one P-graded Fock module: all weights lie in Lambda0-Q+, independent simple roots fix size at a given label weight, and finitely many partitions have that size; the top weight is the single vacuum line. The lattice direct sum embeds the basic residue space in the ambient residue space.
